items.str: From statistical approximation to large language models
This note is addressed to mathematicians.
Its central object is a parameterized family of
conditional probability distributions on finite sequences, constructed from compositions of finite-
dimensional nonlinear maps and determined by numerical minimization of a statistical functional.
We start with the general inverse and approximation problem, then derive the particular architecture,
dimensional bookkeeping, objective functional, and differentiation rules needed to understand
contemporary language models. Conventional machine-learning names are collected at the end
of each mathematical setup, rather than used as prerequisites. All logarithms are natural, and
vectors are columns unless explicitly represented as rows of a matrix.

What the statistical objective can and cannot establish
The conditional distribution identity shows that minimizing the expected logarithmic discrepancy
seeks a probability law under a prescribed prefix distribution. For unrestricted conditional laws, its
exact minimizer is the true law almost everywhere. In a restricted family and with finite observations,
neither exact recovery nor uniform control follows solely from a small observed objective.

Finally, the probability of an utterance under a text distribution is not the probability that its
mathematical or factual assertion is true. A low discrepancy on text does not prove sound reasoning,
nor does it establish that internal coordinate axes correspond to identifiable concepts. In particular,
equivalent coordinate representations and parameter symmetries make parameter interpretation
The independent evaluation collection is a test set (a validation set is used to select
configurations). The exponential of mean cross-entropy is perplexity. A change in the law of observed
inputs is distribution shift; a plausible but unsupported output is often called a hallucination.
The entire mathematical construction can be compressed into the following chain:
The first line and its continuation describe evaluation of a conditional probability family. The second
chain describes determination of its adjustable coefficients. The first is a composition of maps on finite-
dimensional spaces; the second is a statistical variational problem solved by numerical differentiation
and minimization. Their dimensions must not be conflated.
The general principles are not peculiar to language: restriction of an underdetermined family,
approximation of expected functionals by finite sums, nonlinear parameterization, and adjoint differ-
entiation recur throughout applied mathematics. The special feature here is the factorization of a
sequence law into conditional laws, together with a shared, lower-triangular nonlinear composition.
